TrueNAS: A Step-by-Step Guide to Dataset and Share Permissions
recent_posts.summary: A step-by-step walkthrough for setting up SMB shares with proper permissions in TrueNAS 26. Covers creating users and groups, creating datasets with SMB presets, configuring ACLs (both default built-in users and custom group-based permissions), applying permissions recursively, and a key gotcha: SMB service must be restarted for group membership changes to take effect. Also touches on advanced share settings like bind IP addresses, access-based enumeration, host allow/deny, and special share types (Time Machine, Final Cut Pro).

recent_posts.title: UniFi Protect local AI camera system setup and features overview
recent_posts.summary: UniFi Protect version 7 offers a local-first security camera platform with AI detection, facial recognition, smart alerts, and no subscription fees. All processing runs on hardware you own, with no footage leaving your network. The review covers hardware selection (NVRs, cameras, AI Key), the Design Center planning tool, real-world features like 'Find Anything' image search, smart zones, loitering detection, audio detection, alarm customization with webhooks, multi-camera synchronized playback, and case management for sharing clips. A Ubiquiti account is optional and only brokers remote access, not footage storage.

recent_posts.title: The VMware Exit Strategy: Proxmox vs. XCP-ng in 2026
recent_posts.summary: Following Broadcom's acquisition of VMware and the resulting pricing and licensing upheaval, businesses are evaluating open source hypervisor alternatives. Proxmox and XCP-ng are the two leading contenders. Proxmox, built on Debian with KVM, benefits from a large community talent pool and modular tooling but requires managing multiple components and lacks enterprise-grade SLA support. XCP-ng, a fork of Citrix XenServer maintained by Vates, offers a purpose-built minimal host OS, a unified management plane (Xen Orchestra), and formal SLA-backed support closer to VMware's model. The key differentiators are TCO, update management complexity, and support guarantees. Proprietary alternatives are dismissed as simply resetting the vendor lock-in clock, while OpenShift is noted as a different category of platform. The recommendation is to choose based on team skill set and formal support requirements.

recent_posts.title: Should You Run Docker in LXC on Proxmox 9?
recent_posts.summary: A practical comparison of running Docker inside LXC containers versus VMs on Proxmox 9.1, covering key trade-offs including kernel isolation, system stability, live migration, network storage (NFS/SMB), GPU passthrough, and resource efficiency. LXC containers use significantly less RAM (158MB vs 600MB for the same workload) and scale dynamically, but share the Proxmox kernel, meaning a kernel panic can crash the entire host. VMs offer stronger isolation and easier NFS/SMB mounts but consume more resources. The post also covers ZFS record size tuning to avoid write amplification with high-IO applications. Recommendations: use VMs for stability, live migration, and NAS-dependent stacks; use LXC for resource-constrained home labs running lightweight, self-contained apps like reverse proxies.

recent_posts.title: TrueNAS 2026 Hardening Guide: Step-by-Step Security
recent_posts.summary: A practical walkthrough of security hardening steps for TrueNAS (version 25.10.2.1), covering user management with role-based access, disabling root, creating read-only admin roles, separating SMB-only users from admin accounts, enabling global two-factor authentication with TOTP, locking down the console with a password prompt, binding the web UI and services (SSH, SMB, NFS) to specific network interfaces, restricting web UI access by IP/subnet, configuring per-share host allow/deny rules, and saving configuration backups. Additional tips include enabling ZFS scrubs and snapshots for ransomware recovery, and using dataset encryption for physical security.

recent_posts.title: Pausing Your VPN Breaks the UniFi Kill Switch
recent_posts.summary: UniFi's VPN kill switch has a non-obvious failure mode: pausing or removing a VPN interface in the UniFi management UI silently breaks the kill switch, causing affected devices to route traffic through the next available interface instead of blocking it. This happens because pausing the VPN removes the interface on the backend, invalidating the policy route without any warning. The kill switch works correctly when a VPN goes down naturally. To properly test the kill switch, use wrong credentials or block the VPN server address rather than pausing or removing the interface.
